\title{A Sequentially Updated, Uncertainty-Calibrated Growth Twin for Maturity Monitoring from Sparse Measurements in Youth Athletes}

% TODO(human): affiliations, corresponding author, funding and ethics statements.
\author{Anirudhha~Veeranagaiah~M and Shreyas~J%
\thanks{Code and run records: project repository; every number in this paper is generated from a run.}}

\markboth{Manuscript draft}{Sequential growth twin for maturity monitoring}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Youth sport programmes estimate each athlete's biological maturity to group players, manage
training load and anticipate growth-related injury, usually with a single equation applied to one
measurement. Such equations carry no uncertainty and do not learn from repeated measurements. We
present a growth twin: a per-athlete Bayesian growth-curve state, learned against a reference
cohort, that is updated after every new measurement, estimates age at peak height velocity (PHV)
with calibrated intervals, gives the probability that the athlete is in the growth spurt now, and
forecasts the next measurement. The timing prior widens with distance from PHV, and conformal
calibration on held-out athletes makes the intervals cover at their nominal level. In five-fold
validation by child on the real Berkeley Child Guidance Study (\TwChildren{} children,
\TwEvaluations{} visit-by-visit evaluations), the twin's error in age at PHV was \TwMAE{}~years
against \TwMooreMAE{} for the Moore equation and \TwMirwaldMAE{} for Mirwald, and fell from
\TwMAEFirst{} after one visit to \TwMAELast{} after \TwMaxVisits{}, while the equation did not
improve. Calibrated intervals covered \TwCovConf{} of cases at nominal \SpecInterval{}, and the
growth-spurt probability discriminated with an AUC of \TwCircaAUC{} against \TwCircaAUCMoore{} for
the equation. In an external cohort of \ChGirls{} girls, the twin's estimate correlated
\ChCorrTwin{} with age at menarche against \ChCorrMoore{} for the equation.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Digital twin, growth curve, peak height velocity, maturity offset, Bayesian hierarchical model,
conformal prediction, youth sport, bio-banding.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{B}{iological} maturity differs by several years between children of the same age,
and youth sport uses it to group players by maturity (bio-banding) \cite{cumming2017biobanding},
to adjust training load, and to anticipate growth-related injuries that cluster around the
adolescent growth spurt \cite{hall2025,oxendale2025}. In practice maturity is estimated from one
measurement with a regression equation for maturity offset, the years from peak height velocity
(PHV) \cite{mirwald2002,moore2015}. These equations regress towards the mean, are least accurate
far from PHV \cite{koziel2018modified,malina2021soccer}, give no statement of uncertainty, and do
not improve when the same athlete is measured again.

Growth-curve models such as SITAR \cite{cole2010sitar} describe each child's curve as a shifted and
stretched version of a shared curve and estimate age at PHV well from long series, but they are
usually fitted retrospectively to complete records. Programmes, by contrast, see a few
measurements at a time and need an answer now.

We call our approach a growth twin: a per-athlete model state that is (i) learned against a
reference cohort, (ii) updated after every new measurement, (iii) reports calibrated uncertainty,
(iv) forecasts the next measurement, and (v) feeds a decision, here whether the athlete is in the
growth spurt. Our contributions are: a marginalised Bayesian SITAR-type twin with a timing prior
whose spread grows with distance from PHV; cross-fold conformal calibration of its intervals; an
out-of-sample, visit-by-visit evaluation on real longitudinal data against the equations used in
practice; robustness to the measurement conditions of real programmes; and an external check.

\section{Methods}

\subsection{Growth model}
For athlete $i$ with stature $y_{ij}$ at age $t_{ij}$,
\begin{equation}
y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \delta_i (t_{ij}-\bar t_i) + h\big((t_{ij}-\beta_i)e^{\gamma_i}\big) + \varepsilon_{ij},
\end{equation}
where $h$ is a natural cubic spline shared by athletes of one sex, $\alpha_i$ shifts size,
$\beta_i$ timing, $\gamma_i$ tempo, $\delta_i$ absorbs a mismatch in velocity, and
$\varepsilon_{ij}$ is measurement error. Size and velocity effects are integrated analytically and
timing and tempo numerically on grids, so athlete effects are drawn exactly given the shared
parameters, and two-valued timing posteriors from short series are represented faithfully. Age at
PHV is the age of the highest interior peak of the athlete's velocity curve.

\emph{Distance-dependent timing prior.} The prior for $\beta_i$ is centred on the Moore estimate
\cite{moore2015} with standard deviation $\sigma_\beta(1+\kappa\,|m_i|)$, where $m_i$ is the Moore
maturity offset at the visit used for the prior and $\kappa$ is learned. This encodes the known
loss of accuracy of the equations far from PHV \cite{koziel2018modified}.

\subsection{The twin: reference cohort and sequential updating}
The shared parameters are learned from a reference cohort's full records. Each reference child's
prior is computed from one random season of its own record, as it would be at deployment, so the
learned prior spread reflects real prior error. A new athlete's twin is then the posterior of its
effects given the shared parameters and the measurements so far; each new visit redraws it.
The shared curve is fitted at its posterior mode, as SITAR fits by maximum likelihood; the
athlete's state remains fully Bayesian given it. One fold was refitted with full MCMC (NUTS) as a
check (Section~\ref{sec:nuts}).

\subsection{Calibration and decision output}
Raw posterior intervals are rescaled by cross-fold, split conformal calibration
\cite{lei2018conformal,angelopoulos2021gentle}: the score is the error in units of the athlete's
posterior standard deviation, and for athletes in fold $k$ the scaling quantile is taken from the
held-out athletes of the other folds with the same number of visits, so no athlete calibrates its
own interval. The same procedure calibrates the \SpecHorizon{}-month stature forecast. The decision
output is the posterior probability that the athlete is within \SpecCircaWidth{}~year of PHV now.

\subsection{Data}
The Berkeley Child Guidance Study \cite{tuddenham1954}, distributed with the \texttt{sitar}
package \cite{sitarpkg}, follows \TwChildren{} children born in 1928--29 with stature, stem
(sitting) height and mass every six months from 8 to 21 years; it was not used to develop the
Moore equations. The reference age at PHV of each child was obtained from the full record by a
Preece--Baines model 1 fit \cite{preece1978} checked against a smoothing spline. The Chard Growth
Study (12 girls measured six-monthly from 8 to 16 years with age at menarche, no sitting height;
also in \texttt{sitar}) served as an external check.

\subsection{Evaluation}
Children were split into \TwFolds{} folds by child, separately by sex. For each fold the twin's
reference curve was learned from the other folds; each held-out child entered at a random
measurement age between 8 and 15 years, and the twin was updated after each of up to
\TwMaxVisits{} six-monthly visits. After each update we recorded age at PHV (against the
Preece--Baines reference and against the same model given the child's whole record, which removes
differences between curve families), interval coverage, the growth-spurt probability, and the
forecast of the next measurement. Comparators used the same visits: Moore and, for boys, Mirwald,
taken at the visit each places closest to PHV; and extrapolation of the last observed velocity for
the forecast. Robustness was tested by degrading only the held-out children's data: yearly instead
of six-monthly visits, added measurement error, and no sitting height (Moore's stature-only
equation for boys). A leg-length extension, in which leg length shares each child's timing with an
individual leg-to-stature lag, was evaluated in the same way.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Accuracy as visits accumulate}
Over \TwEvaluations{} evaluations the twin's mean absolute error in age at PHV was \TwMAE{}~years
against \TwMooreMAE{} for Moore and \TwMirwaldMAE{} for Mirwald (Table~\ref{tab:visits},
Fig.~\ref{fig:sequential}). It fell from \TwMAEFirst{} after the first visit to \TwMAELast{} after
\TwMaxVisits{}; the equation, which does not learn from repeated visits, stayed between
\TwMooreFirst{} and \TwMooreLast{}. Against the twin's own full-record estimate the errors were
\TwMAEFull{} and \TwMooreMAEFull{}~years, and the twin's bias fell from \TwBiasPB{} (against
Preece--Baines) to \TwBiasFull{}~years, showing that the bias against the Preece--Baines reference
is a difference between curve families. The twin was more accurate than Moore in \TwBandsBetter{}
of \TwBands{} bands of distance from PHV (Table~\ref{tab:bands}); the exception was the band
\TwWorstBand{} years before PHV (\TwWorstBandTwin{} against \TwWorstBandMoore{}~years).

\subsection{Calibrated uncertainty}
Raw nominal \SpecInterval{} intervals covered \TwCovRaw{} of cases (mean width \TwWidthRaw{}~years);
after conformal calibration they covered \TwCovConf{} (width \TwWidthConf{}). The learned timing
prior widened by \TwSlope{} of its standard deviation per year of distance from PHV.

\subsection{Is the athlete in the growth spurt now?}
\TwCircaPrev{} of evaluations were within \SpecCircaWidth{}~year of PHV. The twin's probability
discriminated these with an AUC of \TwCircaAUC{}, against \TwCircaAUCMoore{} for the Moore offset.
At a probability of one half the twin's sensitivity and specificity were \TwCircaSensTwin{} and
\TwCircaSpecTwin{}, against \TwCircaSensMoore{} and \TwCircaSpecMoore{} for the usual rule of an
offset within one year.

\subsection{Forecasting the next measurement}
The twin's \SpecHorizon{}-month forecast error was \TwForecastMAESame{}~cm against \TwNaiveMAE{} for
extrapolating the last observed velocity on the same visits, so the twin forecasts about as well
as the simplest practical rule while also quantifying its uncertainty: calibrated forecast
intervals covered \TwForecastCovConf{} of measurements (raw \TwForecastCovRaw{}) with a width of
\TwForecastWidthConf{}~cm.

\subsection{Robustness and model variants}
Table~\ref{tab:variants} shows the twin under the measurement conditions of real programmes and
with the leg-length extension. With yearly visits the error was \TwYearlyMAE{}~years (Moore
\TwYearlyMoore{}); with one centimetre of added measurement error \TwNoiseMAE{} (Moore
\TwNoiseMoore{}); without sitting height \TwNosittingMAE{} (Moore stature-only \TwNosittingMoore{}).
Calibrated coverage stayed at \TwYearlyCov{}, \TwNoiseCov{} and \TwNosittingCov{}. Adding leg length
did not help: \TwLegSharedMAE{}~years with shared timing and \TwLegLagMAE{} with an individual lag,
against \TwMainMAE{} for stature alone.

\subsection{Full MCMC check}\label{sec:nuts}
Refitting the shared curve of one fold by NUTS gave an error of \TwNutsMAE{}~years and raw coverage
\TwNutsCov{}, against \TwMapFoldMAE{} and \TwMapFoldCov{} with the posterior mode on the same
children (largest R-hat \TwNutsRhat{}, smallest bulk effective sample size \TwNutsESS{}).

\subsection{External check}
Trained on all Berkeley girls and applied visit by visit to the \ChGirls{} Chard girls, the twin's
final estimate differed from the full-record age at PHV by \ChTwinMAE{}~years against \ChMooreMAE{}
for Moore (\ChRef{} girls with a full-record reference). In the \ChMen{} girls with observed
menarche, the twin's age at PHV correlated \ChCorrTwin{} with age at menarche (Moore \ChCorrMoore{}),
and menarche followed the twin's PHV by \ChLagMean{}~years (SD \ChLagSD{}; Moore \ChMooreLagSD{}),
consistent with the known interval between the two.

\section{Discussion}
A growth twin that learns from each new measurement estimates maturity timing substantially better
than the equations used in practice, and its advantage grows with every visit, which is how
programmes actually collect data. Its intervals, once conformally calibrated, mean what they say,
and its growth-spurt probability is a better basis for decisions such as bio-banding or
load-management alerts than an equation's offset. The twin is not better everywhere: one to three
years before PHV, where a season of steady childhood growth says little about when the spurt will
come, the equation was as good or better, and the calibrated interval is correspondingly wide.

Two negative results are informative. The six-month forecast was only on a par with velocity
extrapolation, so the twin's value lies in timing and uncertainty, not short-term prediction of
stature. And leg length, despite the known earlier peak of the legs, did not improve the estimate:
the lag between leg and stature growth varies between children enough to offset the information
it carries.

\emph{Limitations.} The development data come from a historical North American cohort and the
external check is small. The twin has not yet been tested in athletes or in Indian children, where
growth timing differs; the code accepts such data directly (Data Availability). The shared curve
was fitted at its posterior mode, with full MCMC checked on one fold.

\section{Conclusion}
A sequentially updated, uncertainty-calibrated growth twin can replace one-off maturity equations
in youth sport programmes: it is more accurate, learns from each visit, says how sure it is, and
answers the question practitioners ask, whether an athlete is in the growth spurt now.

\section*{Data and Code Availability}
Berkeley and Chard data: \texttt{sitar} R package (CRAN). Code, configuration and run records are
in the project repository; every number in this paper is generated from a run and traceable to its
